tagline: Read real texts, click unknown words, watch your known-word count grow.
verdictSummary: LingQ is the one entry in this category whose content is meant to be yours: the method is importing texts you care about and marking words by status. That mechanic — tokenise, colour by status, click to look up, count what you know — is a weekend. What the subscription adds is the imported library, the dictionaries wired in per language, and clients that work on a phone during a commute.
coreLoopDIY: Import any text, see every word coloured by whether you know it, click unknown ones to look them up and save them, and track your known-word count over time.
whatYouLose: the library of imported lessons with matched audio
dictionary lookups wired up per language, including community definitions
the mobile apps, where most reading actually happens
tutors and conversation sessions bought with points
browser and video importers that handle awkward sources
whyPeopleStillPay: Fifteen dollars buys a method that already works on a phone with dictionaries in place, and the setup you avoid is exactly the setup this build asks for.
prompt:
Build a reading tool that tracks word knowledge across everything you read in a target language.

Import plain text, EPUB and subtitle files. Tokenise with a real tokeniser for the language rather than splitting on spaces — this matters enormously outside western European languages and quietly matters inside them too, for contractions and clitics. Lemmatise where a lemmatiser exists, and store both surface form and lemma.

Every token gets a status: unknown, learning with a level from one to four, known, or ignored (names, numbers). Status is stored per lemma and applies everywhere, so a word you learned in one book is already coloured in the next. Render the text with each word coloured by status; clicking one opens a definition pane and sets its status.

Definitions come from an offline dictionary file you supply. Wiktionary extracts are published in machine-readable form under a free licence for most major languages — parse one into SQLite at import time rather than calling an online dictionary on every click.

The number that makes the method work is known words over time, so store a daily snapshot and plot it. Add a per-text statistic shown before you start reading: percentage of tokens already known. Below about ninety-five percent, reading is decoding rather than reading, and knowing that in advance changes what you pick.

Saved words export to Anki-compatible TSV with the sentence they came from, so review happens in a tool that already has mobile clients.

Do not build audio alignment between a text and a recording. Getting it right needs forced alignment and careful handling of mismatched editions, and it is a project of its own.

faq.q: Can I import my LingQ words?
faq.a: Yes, and this is the rare good case: LingQ exports your saved words with their status and context sentence as CSV. Map status to your own scale and import directly — your known-word count carries over, which is the number the whole method runs on.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: Only through a mobile browser if you host it. Reading is the part of language learning that most naturally happens on a phone, so this is the gap you will feel; exporting saved words to Anki covers the review half at least.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing beyond hosting if you want it away from your desk. Dictionary data is a one-off download, and there is no API in the loop.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Material at your level, ready to open. LingQ's library is graded and comes with audio; your version is only as good as the texts you can find and are able to read.
